title: Collisions:  If This, Then That
tagline: Things finally touch each other, and your program decides what happens next.  This is where it becomes a game.
timing: Two periods.  Day 1:  touch the coin, score a point.  Day 2:  a hazard, and a game that can end.
newIdea: `if` -- making something happen only when it is true.  Collisions give it something to be true about.
builtOn: Lesson 5 -- your world, with a coin drifting through it.
goals: Use `collidesWith()` to find out whether your player is touching something
Use an `if` statement so something happens only when it is true
Keep score with a variable that changes, and show it on screen with `text()`
Use a `boolean` to switch your game between two **states**:  playing and game over

vocab.def: asks "are these two sprites touching?" and gives back `true` or `false`
"if this is true, do this block of code"
the yes-or-no question inside the parentheses of an `if`
the invisible circle used to decide if something is touching.  For your character it is the radius in the `super(...)` line
a named box for a value.  `int score = 0;` makes a box called score that starts at zero
a variable that holds a whole number -- 0, 7, -3.  No decimals
a variable that is only ever `true` or `false`
a Processing function that draws words or numbers on the screen
which mode your program is in right now -- playing, or game over

warmup: **Day 1:**  your world has a coin drifting through it, and touching it does nothing.  What *should* happen?  **Day 2:**  name a game where touching the wrong thing ends it.  How does the game tell you it is over?

howItWorks.h: Day 1 - collidesWith() asks a yes-or-no question
p: The library checks whether two circles overlap and hands you back `true` or `false`.  That is exactly the kind of answer an `if` is built to use.

code.label: Flash the sky gold while you touch the coin

bullets: The part in the parentheses is the **condition**.  When it is true, the code inside the braces runs.  When it is false, Processing skips straight past the braces.
This works because you wrote `class MyCharacter extends Blob` back in Lesson 2.  Your character got `collidesWith()` for free, and you never had to write it.

howItWorks.h: Your hitbox is the radius you set in Lesson 2
p: Remember the `30` in your `super(...)` line?  That is the invisible circle the collision check uses.  The collision check reads that number and only that number, so your drawing can be any size you like.

A **bigger** radius means collisions trigger from further away, which feels generous and forgiving.  A **smaller** radius means you have to be right on top of something, which feels precise and harsh.
If your collisions feel wrong, that number is what to change.

howItWorks.h: A variable that remembers the score
p: A score has to **remember** something from one frame to the next.  So it goes at the very **top** of your sketch, outside `setup()` and outside `draw()`.

code.label: At the top, next to your other variables

bullets: Written up there, **every** function can see it.
Written inside `setup()`, it vanishes the second `setup()` finishes, and `draw()` cannot see it at all.

p: `text()` draws words.  You give it what to say and where to put it.

code.label: Showing the score
code.body:
fill(50);                          // the text color
textSize(24);                      // how big
text("Score: " + score, 20, 36);   // what, then x, then y

bullets: The `+` glues the words `"Score: "` and the number `score` together into one piece of text.
Set `fill()` **before** `text()`, or your text takes whatever color the last shape used.

howItWorks.h: Why the score races, and the fix
p: Put `score = score + 1;` inside the `if` and sit your player on the coin.  The score climbs about sixty points a second.
Here is why.  `draw()` runs sixty times a second, so it asks "are they touching?" sixty times a second.  For as long as you sit there, the answer is yes, and every yes is a point.
The fix is to end the touch the moment you count it.  Move the coin somewhere else.

code.label: One touch, one point

bullets: `moveTo(x, y)` picks a sprite up and puts it down somewhere else.
`random()` from Lesson 3 picks the spot, so the coin lands somewhere new every time.

howItWorks.h: Day 2 - a hazard, and a boolean
p: A hazard is one more `Blob`, red and fast, with its own `if`.  Touching it has to end the game, and the game needs a way to remember that it has ended.
That is the job for a `boolean`, the simplest variable there is.  It is `true` or it is `false`.

code.label: At the top, and in your game code

p: This is the big idea of Day 2.  Your game is always in a **mode**.  Right now there are two:  playing, and game over.

The `boolean gameOver` remembers which mode you are in, and an `if/else` in `draw()` picks which one to run.  `!` means **NOT**, so `!gameOver` reads as "not game over" -- in other words, "still playing."

code.label: Two states, one choice

bullets: `playGame()` and `showGameOver()` are functions you write yourself.  Your game code moves into `playGame()`, and the game over screen goes in `showGameOver()`.
Leave the scenery in `draw()`, above the `if`, so your world shows behind both screens.

p: A condition can compare numbers too.  This is how you would make something happen at a score.

code.label: A question about a number

bullets: `>` greater than, `<` less than, `>=` at least, `<=` at most, `==` exactly equal.
Careful:  `==` is a question ("are these equal?").  A single `=` is a command ("make this equal to that").  Mixing them up is a classic.

steps: ### Day 1 - touch the coin, score a point
Open your Lesson 5 sketch.
In `draw()`, right after your `background()` line, add `if (player.collidesWith(coin)) { background(255, 220, 50); }`.  Run it and touch the coin.  The sky flashes gold while you touch it.
If touching feels too hard or too easy, open your `MyCharacter` tab and change the radius in the `super(...)` line.
Delete the flash.  At the very top of your sketch, add `int score = 0;`
At the bottom of `draw()`, add the three lines that show the score:  `fill(50);`, `textSize(24);`, and `text("Score: " + score, 20, 36);`.  Run it.  You should see `Score: 0` in the corner.
Test it by cheating:  change `int score = 0;` to `int score = 7;` and run.  The display should change.  Set it back to 0.
Above the score lines, add the collision `if` again, this time with `score = score + 1;` inside it.  Run it and sit on the coin.  Watch the score.  Why is it doing that?
Add `coin.moveTo(random(width), random(100, height - 150));` inside the same `if`.  Run it.  One touch, one point.
Make it yours:  change the coin's speed and size, and style the score so it fits your world.
### Day 2 - a game that can end
Open your Day 1 sketch.  (If it is broken, paste in the Day 1 checkpoint below and keep your own `MyCharacter` and `Cloud` tabs.)
Declare `Blob hazard;` at the top.  In `setup()`, create it in a corner, away from your player:  `hazard = new Blob(this, 80, 80, 22, 3, 2, color(220, 60, 60));`.  Move and draw it in `draw()`.
At the top, add `boolean gameOver = false;`
Add `if (player.collidesWith(hazard)) { gameOver = true; }`.  Run it and touch the hazard.  Nothing seems to happen.  The variable changed -- and nothing in your sketch reads it yet.

Make a new function called `playGame()` below `draw()`.  Move your coin, hazard, player, both collision `if`s, and the score display into it.  In `draw()`, after the scenery, call `playGame();`.  Run it.  Nothing should look different, and that means it worked.
Write a `showGameOver()` function.  Copy it from the starter code below.
In `draw()`, replace `playGame();` with the `if (!gameOver) { playGame(); } else { showGameOver(); }` block.  Run it and touch the hazard.  Game over.
Test the other branch by cheating:  change `boolean gameOver = false;` to `true` and run.  You should land straight on the game over screen.  Set it back.
Make it yours:  rewrite the game over screen so it sounds like your game, tune the hazard, and add a second one if you want a harder game.

makeItYours: Add a second hazard, `hazard2`, with its own `if`.  Give it a different speed or size.
Add a second coin, `coin2`, that is worth more:  `score = score + 5;`
Change what ends the game.  A hazard?  Reaching a score of 20?  Both?
Restyle the game over screen -- different words, different colors, a message that fits your game.
Make the background change as the score goes up -- a few `if` statements stacked up, one for each score.
challenge: Give the player lives.  Start with `int lives = 3;`.  When the hazard hits, take one away and move the hazard somewhere else (exactly like the coin).  Only set `gameOver` to `true` when `lives` reaches 0.  Show the lives on screen next to the score.
flintHint: Good things to ask:  "my score goes up way too fast", "my score will not show up on screen", "what is the difference between = and ==?", or "how do I add a second hazard?"  Paste your `draw()` or `playGame()` in if something will not run.
wrapup: **Day 1:**  why did the score race upward before you added `moveTo()`?  **Day 2:**  what is the difference between an `int` and a `boolean`?  Give an example of each from your own game.
assignmentTask: Make things in your world interact.  The player touches something, and your program decides what happens.
assignmentDo: Use `collidesWith()` inside an `if` so touching the coin scores a point.
Keep the score in a variable at the top of your sketch and show it with `text()`.
Add a hazard, and use a `boolean` with an `if/else` to switch between playing and game over.
Make it yours.  The coin, the hazard, and the game over screen should all belong to your world.  Rewrite the starter's "Game Over" in words that fit your game.
submit: A short screen recording showing a coin being collected and the game ending.
Your answer to **Show your thinking** below.
checklist: Keep a score with an `int` and show it with `text()`.
Use a `boolean` and an `if/else` to switch between playing and game over.
Explain why the coin has to jump away when it is collected.
standard: Use `collidesWith()` inside `if` statements to trigger game events, track the score with a variable shown by `text()`, and use a `boolean` to switch between playing and game over.

stages.name: Getting Started
stages.text: Collisions are not registering, my score will not show, or it races up too fast.  **Next step:**  put the `if (player.collidesWith(coin))` check inside `draw()` (or `playGame()`), declare `score` at the **top** of the sketch, and move the coin away with `moveTo()` the moment it is collected.

stages.name: Got It Working
stages.text: Touching the coin scores one point and the coin jumps away.  The score shows on screen.  Touching the hazard switches to a game over screen.

stages.name: Made It Mine
stages.text: …and I made the rules mine -- a second hazard, a coin worth more, a different way for the game to end, or a game over screen that sounds like my game.

stages.name: Went Beyond
stages.text: …and I layered rules of my own on top:  lives that count down, a background that changes with the score, or another idea of mine that makes the game react.

thinking: In one or two sentences:  what happens in your game when the player touches something -- and why does the coin have to jump away?

di.h: Day 1 - start with the question the room is already asking
p: Lesson 5 left a coin drifting through every student's world, and touching it does nothing.  Open with that.  Ask what *should* happen, take two or three answers, then show that the library can already answer "are they touching?"

The `if` arrives as the way to act on the answer.  That order is the point of this lesson:  the collision first, then the decision about it.  Every `if` a student writes here has something real to be about.

di.h: collidesWith() - and why they already have it
p: "The library checks whether the two circles overlap and returns true or false."

Make the connection explicit:  **because `MyCharacter extends Blob`**, their character can use `collidesWith()` against any other Blob.  This is the payoff for the one-word decision back in Lesson 2, and it is worth naming so `extends` feels like it earned its keep.
Leave the word *inheritance* out.

`if (player.collidesWith(coin)) { background(255, 220, 50); }`, right after the sky.  It is the smallest possible `if` with the loudest possible result, and every student sees their own `if` work within the first ten minutes.
Say the shape out loud:  condition in the parentheses, action in the braces, and the action runs only when the condition is true.

di.h: The hitbox is the radius from super()
p: Circle back to the `30` in their Lesson 2 constructor.  That is the collision circle, and it is separate from how big their art looks.
A big radius is forgiving; a small one is precise.  Students whose character art drifted far from their radius will get collisions that feel wrong, and this is the fix.

di.h: Global scope - say why as well as where
p: `int score = 0;` goes above `setup()`.  "It lives outside `setup()` and `draw()` so every function can see it."

Students will try to declare it inside `setup()`.  When they do, the variable disappears the instant `setup()` ends.  Show that failure once if you have time -- the error message is hard to read cold.

di.h: Let the score race, then fix it
p: Put `score = score + 1;` inside the `if` and let students sit on the coin.  The score climbs about sixty a second.  Ask why before you explain.
`draw()` asks the question every frame, and the answer is yes for every frame they overlap.  `moveTo()` fixes it by ending the overlap the moment it is counted.
This is the highest-value few minutes of Day 1.  Students learn that `draw()` keeps asking, and they learn it from their own score.
`fill(50); textSize(24); text("Score: " + score, 20, 36);`
"The `+` here glues text and a number together into one string."  Skip the word *concatenation*.
Point out that `fill()` has to come **before** `text()`, or the text inherits whatever color the last shape used.  This will bite someone.

di.h: Day 2 - a hazard that changes a variable
p: Add the hazard and the `if` that sets `gameOver = true`.  Run it, and let students notice that touching the hazard *looks* like nothing.
The variable changed, and nothing reads it yet.  That gap is the reason for the `if/else` in `draw()`, so let the room sit in it for a moment before you fill it.
`if (!gameOver) { playGame(); } else { showGameOver(); }`
"`!` means NOT -- so `if not gameOver` means `if the game is still going`."
This is the structural idea of Day 2.  The game has **modes**, a variable remembers which one, and `draw()` picks.  Lesson 7 adds a third mode for winning and builds everything on this shape.
Worth thirty explicit seconds, best attached to a score condition like `if (score >= 10)`.  A single `=` **assigns**; a double `==` **asks**.  Write both on the board.
In Java the compiler will usually catch `if (score = 10)`, which is a mercy, but students need the vocabulary to read the error.
Day 1:  flash → score variable → score on screen → score changes on contact → coin jumps away.  Day 2:  hazard → boolean → `playGame()` → `if/else` with `showGameOver()`.
Run after every arrow.  Pasting the whole finished structure at once hides where each piece came from.

guided: Warm-up:  what should happen when you touch the coin?  Take a few answers.
Everyone adds the flash `if` right after `background()`.  Run.  Everyone touches their coin.  Let the room react.
Anyone whose collisions feel wrong:  open `MyCharacter` and tune the radius in `super(...)`.
Replace the flash with the score:  the global variable, then the `text()` lines.  Run.  `Score: 0` appears.
**Test by cheating:**  `int score = 7;`, run, set it back.  Testing a display by hand-setting the value is a real technique and worth naming.
Add `score = score + 1;` inside the collision `if`.  Let them sit on the coin.  Ask why the score races before you explain it.
Release for personalization:  coin speed and size, score styling, a second coin worth five.
Warm-up:  a game where touching the wrong thing ends it.  If anyone missed Day 1, they paste in the Day 1 checkpoint now.
Add the hazard and the `gameOver` boolean together.  Add the hazard `if`.  Run.  Touching it seems to do nothing.  Ask why.
Refactor together:  move the game code from `draw()` into `playGame()`.  Run -- nothing should change.  Say it plainly:  a refactor that changes nothing visible is a *success*.
Add the `if/else` in `draw()` and write `showGameOver()`.  Run and touch the hazard.
**Test the other branch by cheating:**  set `gameOver = true` in the declaration and run.  Straight to the game over screen.  Set it back.
Release for personalization:  a second hazard, a restyled game over screen, lives for the fast finishers.
pitfalls: **The racing score** -- the collision `if` adds a point every frame because nothing ends the overlap.  It is the Day 1 lesson.  `moveTo()` fixes it.
**Putting the collision `if` in `setup()`.**  It is checked once, before anything moves, and never again.
**Declaring `score` or `gameOver` inside `setup()`.**  Scope error.  The most common structural mistake in this lesson.
**`fill()` after `text()`** -- text comes out in an unexpected color.

**`textAlign(CENTER, CENTER)` never reset.**  It affects every later `text()` call.  The starter resets it with `textAlign(LEFT, BASELINE)` at the end of `showGameOver()` -- make sure students who restyle that function keep the reset.
**A hazard created on top of the player**, so the game ends the instant it starts.  The starter puts the hazard in a corner for exactly this reason.
**Scenery moved into `playGame()`** during the refactor, so the world vanishes behind the game over screen.  Harmless, and worth asking the student whether that is what they want.
Collisions that never fire because the character's radius is tiny compared to the art.
Forgetting the braces on a one-line `if` and then adding a second line later that runs every frame.
teacher.wrapupAnswer: **Day 1:**  `draw()` asks the question every frame, and the answer is yes for every frame the two overlap, so one touch scored many points.  `moveTo()` ends the overlap the moment it is counted.  **Day 2:**  an `int` holds a whole number (score, lives); a `boolean` holds only true or false (gameOver).  Look for examples from their own sketch.
notes: This lesson replaces the old Lesson 6 (If This, Then That) and Lesson 7 (Collisions!).  The old Lesson 6 taught `if` with a score that nothing could change, so the starter did nothing visible when it ran.  Here every `if` has a collision to be about from the first ten minutes.

Two days, one new idea.  `if` is the concept.  `collidesWith()`, `int`, `boolean`, and `text()` are the supporting cast.  If a student is struggling, drop the `playGame()` refactor and get an `if/else` working directly in `draw()`.
The Day 1 checkpoint is on the page for anyone who missed Day 1 or whose sketch is broken when Day 2 starts.  Paste it in, keep their own `MyCharacter` and `Cloud` tabs, and they are caught up.
`score++` is shorthand for `score = score + 1`.  Fine to mention if a student asks, but keep `score = score + 1` in the starter, so students can see the operation written out.
The "test by cheating" move (hand-setting a variable to check a branch) is a genuine debugging skill.  Name it while you use it.
Radius tuning is a real design decision.  Frame it that way:  "do you want your game generous or precise?"
Fast finishers:  lives, a second hazard, a coin worth five.  Students who ask for *lots* of coins are ready for Bonus Lesson D.
This is the lesson where the moving picture becomes a **game**.  Expect energy, and leave time to play.
